subject: fix: only treat None and 0 as "no wait" (#741)
problem_statement:
fix: only treat None and 0 as "no wait" (#741)

BaseRetrying skipped the wait strategy whenever it was falsy, so a
callable strategy that is an empty container or defines __bool__ was
never called. Match the "no wait" values (None, 0, and sum([]) over no
strategies) explicitly, and replace them with wait_none() at construction
so both the sync and async loops just call the strategy. This drops the
truthy-bool type: ignore in both _run_wait.

Supersedes #731.


Change-Id: Ic5b013f36c168a6c387ad912840c4ab944c72f4b

subject: Respect enabled=False on the direct-call path (#645)
problem_statement:
Respect enabled=False on the direct-call path (#645)

* fix: respect enabled=False when calling the controller directly

`Retrying.__call__` and `AsyncRetrying.__call__` ignored the `enabled`
flag: calling a controller created with `enabled=False` still ran the
full retry loop, so a failing function was retried and the original
exception was wrapped in a `RetryError`.

This makes the direct-call protocol consistent with the decorator
(`@retry(enabled=False)`) and the iterator protocols
(`__iter__`/`__aiter__`, fixed in #643): with `enabled=False` the
function is executed exactly once and any exception propagates
unchanged.

* fix(types): correct type-ignore codes in asyncio early-return path

subject: fix: read the tornado global live instead of an import-time snapshot (#696)
problem_statement:
fix: read the tornado global live instead of an import-time snapshot (#696)

#679 replaced `if tornado:` with a `_HAS_TORNADO` bool computed once at
import, to stop `truthy-bool` flagging the module object as always true.
But only one of the two call sites was converted: the `retry()` decorator
still dereferences the live `tornado` global right after testing the
snapshot. The two desync as soon as anything reassigns the global.

A/B verified against a2af454: `tenacity.tornado = None` followed by any
`@tenacity.retry` decoration returned normally before, and now raises
`AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'gen'`. Nulling the
module global is the standard way a downstream suite exercises the
non-tornado path without uninstalling tornado.

Replace the constant with a `_has_tornado()` function so both call sites
read the live global and cannot drift apart. As a bonus this needs no
`redundant-expr` suppression: the check reads as a plain return rather than
the left operand of an `and`.

Change-Id: I6f0fbb9cad3d4e46599b0cae1b5b60378742fd1f

subject: fix: restore support for falsy wait values and callable + strategy (#694)
problem_statement:
fix: restore support for falsy wait values and callable + strategy (#694)

Three runtime regressions from the mypy-strictness stack (#679, #677), all
A/B verified against a2af454. None were caught by the test suite, and all
three only fire once a retry actually happens, so happy-path callers see
nothing until production.

1. `Retrying(wait=None)`, `wait=0` and `wait=sum([])` now raise
   `TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not callable` from inside `iter()`.
   #679 removed the `if self.wait:` guard on the grounds that `truthy-bool`
   proved it always true -- but that only holds for the *declared* type.
   Untyped callers pass `None`/`0` to mean "no wait", and `sum([])` over an
   empty strategy list returns the int 0. The `TypeError` is raised outside
   the attempt's try/except, so it escapes uncaught and destroys the caller's
   real exception. Restore the guard with a local `truthy-bool` suppression
   explaining why the "impossible" branch is reachable. `before`, `after`,
   `before_sleep` and `retry_error_callback` all kept their `is not None`
   guards; `wait` was the only one dropped.

2. `plain_callable + wait_strategy` now raises `TypeError`. `WaitBaseT`
   admits plain callables, and a function has no `__add__`, so this went
   through `wait_base.__radd__` -- which #677 narrowed to `int`. Widen it to
   `WaitBaseT | int` and build the `wait_combine` again. `5 + strategy` is
   still rejected, now via `NotImplemented` rather than a combination that
   fails later. The parameter stays `int` rather than `Literal[0]` because
   typeshed's `sum()` protocol requires `__radd__(x: int)`; narrowing it
   would make every `sum()` over strategies need a `type: ignore`.

3. `wait_combine.__call__` passed the state as `retry_state=`, which crashes
   on any `WaitBaseT` callable whose parameter has another name. Pass it
   positionally, as `BaseRetrying._run_wait` already does.

Adds regression tests for all three plus the async path -- the original
change shipped with no test covering any of them.

Change-Id: Ia40c32a22cdac09cbfba4280fb0a7f0c2cb7b7e0

subject: fix: annotate wait_base.__radd__ as taking the int seed from sum() (#677)
problem_statement:
fix: annotate wait_base.__radd__ as taking the int seed from sum() (#677)

* ci: run on pull requests targeting any base branch

`on.pull_request.branches` filters on the *base* branch, not the head. With
it pinned to `main`, only a pull request merging directly into `main` ran
CI -- every stacked pull request, whose base is the branch below it in the
stack, got no test, lint or mypy run at all and showed nothing but the
Mergify checks.

Drop the filter so CI runs for every pull request regardless of base.

Change-Id: I1c211a106a57b9f4986bec4b76c0680c1a0f1b61

* fix: annotate wait_base.__radd__ as taking the int seed from sum()

`__radd__` was annotated `other: wait_base`, which is the one type it can
never receive: `wait_base.__add__` always succeeds, so Python never falls
back to the reflected operator for two wait strategies. The only caller is
`sum()`, which seeds its accumulator with the int 0 — hence the
`type: ignore[comparison-overlap]` on `other == 0`, and the dead
`return self` branch behind it that `--warn-unreachable` flags.

Annotate the parameter as `int` and return `NotImplemented` for a non-zero
left operand, so `5 + wait_fixed(1)` raises `TypeError` at the addition
rather than building a `wait_combine` that explodes later when called.

With the signature corrected, mypy infers `sum([...])` over wait strategies
on its own, so four `type: ignore[list-item]` comments in
`test_wait_arbitrary_sum` are no longer needed.

Change-Id: Iad1bcef4412d6afc1a6f1335970cfbfcc4a34fcb

subject: Fix static typing of @retry decorated instance methods (fixes #532) (#668)
problem_statement:
Fix static typing of @retry decorated instance methods (fixes #532) (#668)

_RetryDecorated had no __get__, so mypy and pyright treated
instance.method the same as the unbound Class.method: an ordinary call
like instance.method(value=1) demanded an explicit self argument and
the return type resolved to Unknown/Any. Add __get__ overloads so
attribute access through an instance returns the bound form with the
correct return type. The runtime object is a real function from
functools.wraps and already binds correctly, so this is purely a
static analysis fix.

subject: fix: stop hanging on cyclic exception __cause__ chains (#660)
problem_statement:
fix: stop hanging on cyclic exception __cause__ chains (#660)

retry_if_exception_cause_type walked __cause__ until None. Legal cycles
such as ``raise e from e`` (or mutual a<->b causes) never terminate, so
the predicate spins at 100% CPU and stop conditions never run.

Track seen exception ids while walking, matching stdlib traceback's
cycle-safe approach. Regression covers self-cause and two-node cycles.

Fixes #658.

subject: Accept empty message in retry_if_exception_message (#651)
problem_statement:
Accept empty message in retry_if_exception_message (#651)

retry_if_exception_message validated its message/match arguments with
truthiness checks (if message and match, if not message and not match).
An empty string is a valid message target — it matches exceptions whose
str() is empty, e.g. a bare RuntimeError() — but 'not message' is True
for '', so retry_if_exception_message(message='') wrongly raised
TypeError('missing 1 required argument'). _check had the same problem:
'if self.message:' skipped the empty-message branch.

Replace the truthiness guards with 'is None' checks so an empty message
is accepted and matched. This makes every message matchable, not every
message except the empty one.

subject: Avoid unnecessary exponential wait computation (#654)
problem_statement:
Avoid unnecessary exponential wait computation (#654)

Once an exponential wait exceeds its configured maximum, calculate the
threshold logarithmically and return the cap without constructing an ever
larger integer power. Add a regression test that rejects power evaluation
past the cap.

Fixes #526

subject: Keep statistics visible when @retry is further wrapped (fixes #519) (#653)
problem_statement:
Keep statistics visible when @retry is further wrapped (fixes #519) (#653)

* Keep statistics visible when @retry is further wrapped

When a @retry-decorated function was wrapped by another decorator that
uses functools.wraps (e.g. a timing decorator), accessing
``func.statistics`` returned an empty ``{}``.

functools.wraps copies the inner wrapper's ``__dict__`` (including the
``statistics`` reference) into the outer wrapper. On each call the inner
wrapper rebound ``wrapped_f.statistics`` to a fresh dict, so the outer
wrapper kept pointing at the original, now-stale, empty dict.

Reuse the same statistics dict in place on every call (clearing it and
sharing it with the per-call copy) instead of rebinding the attribute.
The dict identity stays stable, so the stats remain reachable through
the outer wrapper's copied ``__dict__``. The same change is applied to
the async wrapper.

Fixes #519.

* Type __wrapped__ on _RetryDecorated so statistics stay type-safe

The runtime fix keeps func.statistics visible when a @retry-decorated
function is further wrapped by another functools.wraps-based decorator.
However mypy (strict) rejected the tests because the public typing did
not expose the attributes the tests rely on:

  * _RetryDecorated had no __wrapped__ member, so accessing
    my_call.__wrapped__.statistics failed with [attr-defined].
  * the sync test's outer decorator was annotated
    Callable[..., Any] -> Callable[..., Any], erasing the
    _RetryDecorated type so .statistics/.__wrapped__ were unreachable.

Declare __wrapped__ on the _RetryDecorated protocol (it is always set by
functools.wraps on the retry wrapper) and make the sync test's outer
decorator type-preserving via a TypeVar, mirroring the async test. mypy,
ruff, pytest and the docs build are all green.

subject: wait_chain: reject empty strategy list with ValueError instead of IndexError (#646)
problem_statement:
wait_chain: reject empty strategy list with ValueError instead of IndexError (#646)

Calling wait_chain() with no strategies stored an empty tuple in
self.strategies. The first call to __call__ then evaluated
min(max(1, 1), 0) == 0, so self.strategies[wait_func_no - 1]
turned into self.strategies[-1] and raised IndexError, which is
opaque for what is really a programmer error at construction time.

Validate in __init__ and raise ValueError('wait_chain() requires
at least one strategy') so the failure happens at the point where
the bad configuration is created, not later when the wait function
is first evaluated inside a running retry.

subject: fix: respect enabled=False in iterator protocols (__iter__ / __aiter__) (#643)
problem_statement:
fix: respect enabled=False in iterator protocols (__iter__ / __aiter__) (#643)

When Retrying(enabled=False) was used with the context-manager iterator
pattern (`for attempt in retrying` / `async for attempt in retrying`),
the `enabled` flag was silently ignored and the full retry machinery ran
(multiple attempts, stop/wait evaluated) instead of executing the body
exactly once and propagating any exception directly.

The `wraps()`-based path already handled `enabled=False` correctly, so
this patch brings the iterator API in line with it:
- BaseRetrying.__iter__: if not enabled, yield one AttemptManager and
  re-raise the stored exception if the attempt failed.
- AsyncRetrying.__aiter__ / __anext__: same semantics via a one-shot
  flag that stops after the first yielded AttemptManager.

Four regression tests are added (two sync, two async) covering the
failure and success cases for each protocol.

subject: Fix ordinal suffix generation for numbers ending in 11, 12, 13 (#556)

The `find_ordinal` utility incorrectly assigned "st", "nd", and "rd" suffixes to numbers greater than 20 that end in 11, 12, or 13 (e.g., 111 became "111st").

subject: fix: compare opaque fragment identifiers verbatim (#806)
problem_statement:
fix: compare opaque fragment identifiers verbatim (#806)

* fix: compare opaque fragment identifiers verbatim

`fragment_identifier_matcher` ran both the required identifier and the request
URL fragment through `parse_qsl`. For an opaque fragment such as `/users/5`
(no `=`), `parse_qsl` returns `[]`, so any two opaque fragments — or a request
with no fragment at all — compared equal. A matcher for `#/users/5` therefore
matched `#/users/6`, `#section2`, and URLs with no fragment.

Only run the order-insensitive `parse_qsl` comparison when the identifier is
query-string-style (contains `=`); otherwise compare the fragment strings
verbatim. Key=value fragments are unaffected.


* Add CHANGES entry for #806

subject: fix: keep blank-valued query params significant in query_string_matcher (#804)
problem_statement:
fix: keep blank-valued query params significant in query_string_matcher (#804)

query_string_matcher parsed both the request and the configured query
with parse_qsl()'s default keep_blank_values=False, so a parameter with
an empty value (b=, or a bare b) was dropped before comparison. As a
result ?a=1 matched a request to ?a=1&b=, and a registration that
required b= matched a request that omitted it.

This auto-applies to any registered URL that carries a query string (via
_should_match_querystring), so it silently mismatches on the default
path. The request-param parser already uses keep_blank_values=True
(__init__.py), so query_param_matcher treats b= as significant — the two
query-matching paths disagreed on the same request. Parse both sides
with keep_blank_values=True so blanks are compared, not discarded.

subject: fix: remove content-type from headers in _add_from_file to avoid RuntimeError (#791)
problem_statement:
fix: remove content-type from headers in _add_from_file to avoid RuntimeError (#791)

* fix: remove content-type from headers in _add_from_file to avoid RuntimeError

The recorder stores content_type as a top-level YAML key but may also
capture a 'content-type' entry inside the headers dict (since HTTP
servers return Content-Type as a response header).

When _add_from_file() calls add() with both content_type= and
headers={'content-type': ...}, add() raises:

    RuntimeError: You cannot define both content_type and
    headers[Content-Type].

Fix: strip any 'content-type' key from headers before calling add()
when content_type is also present in the loaded response dict.  The
content_type kwarg takes precedence, which is already documented as
the recommended approach.

Fixes #741

* test: add regression test for Content-Type conflict in _add_from_file

Fixes the case where a YAML fixture has Content-Type in both headers
and content_type fields — the recorder captures both, causing RuntimeError
when _add_from_file calls add(). Added test_add_from_file_content_type_in_headers
to verify the fix works end-to-end with a YAML fixture.

* test: use mismatched Content-Type values to verify content_type precedence

Per markstory's review: using different values for headers['Content-Type']
('text/html') and content_type ('application/json'/'text/plain') makes the
assertion non-trivial — it now explicitly verifies that content_type wins
over the conflicting header, not just that both happen to carry the same value.

* fix(test): use .yaml extension so _add_from_file selects YAML loader

As suggested by @markstory — the fixture file needs an explicit extension
so that _add_from_file can detect the correct loader. Changed out_file
to use a .yaml suffix for the content_type_in_headers test.

* fix(test): clean up .yaml/.toml fixture variants in teardown_method

The content_type test creates response_record.yaml but teardown_method
only deleted response_record (no extension). Add cleanup for .yaml and
.toml variants to avoid stale artifacts across test runs.

* fix(test): restore _parse_response_file in teardown + reformat for black

Root cause of the CI failure: test_add_from_file[tomli_w] monkey-patches
responses.mock._parse_response_file to a TOML loader and never restores
it, so test_add_from_file_content_type_in_headers inherits the TOML
parser and chokes on the YAML fixture (tomllib.TOMLDecodeError).

The prior fixes (.yaml extension, .yaml/.toml teardown cleanup) don't
help because _parse_response_file always calls yaml.safe_load regardless
of file extension — the bug is in test state leakage, not the loader
dispatch.

- teardown_method: always reset _parse_response_file back to the class
  default so any per-test monkey-patch is contained.
- __init__.py: black wrap for the Content-Type-stripping dict comp
  (was 91 chars, over the 88-char limit).

* fix(test): unwind mock inside test_add_from_file instead of teardown

per markstory's review: capture the original `_parse_response_file`
before monkey-patching it for the tomli_w parametrize variant, then
restore it in a finally block so the mock is contained to the test
that introduces it. removes the class-wide reset from teardown_method
that was leaking responsibility upward.

subject: Make `assert_all_requests_are_fired` always assert on exception (#782)
problem_statement:
Make `assert_all_requests_are_fired` always assert on exception (#782)

* Add assert_on_exception parameter to RequestsMock

When set to True, assertions about unfired requests will be raised even
when an exception occurs in the context manager. This provides valuable
debugging context about which mocked requests were or weren't called
when debugging test failures.

By default (assert_on_exception=False), the assertion is suppressed to
avoid masking the original exception.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)


* Add decorator support for assert_on_exception

The @responses.activate decorator now accepts an assert_on_exception
parameter, providing a convenient way to enable assertion checking
even when exceptions occur:

    @responses.activate(
        assert_all_requests_are_fired=True,
        assert_on_exception=True
    )
    def test_my_api():
        ...

subject: fix: return a parsed PyJWKSet from the JWK Set cache (#1208)
problem_statement:
fix: return a parsed PyJWKSet from the JWK Set cache (#1208)

* fix: return cached PyJWKSet from PyJWKClient.get_jwk_set

`JWKSetCache.put()` documents `PyJWKSet` as the cached value, so callers
can pre-populate the JWK Set cache (e.g. from an externally stored JWKS)
to skip the network round-trip. `get_jwk_set()` only accepted a `dict`
from the cache, so a cache hit holding a `PyJWKSet` raised a misleading
`PyJWKClientError("The JWKS endpoint did not return a JSON object")`,
even though no endpoint call was involved.

Return cached `PyJWKSet` values directly, and widen the cache type hints
to `PyJWKSet | dict` so they describe what is actually stored -
`fetch_data()` caches the raw JSON payload it fetched, while callers
populating the cache themselves store a `PyJWKSet`. Other invalid cache
values still raise `PyJWKClientError` as before.

Fixes #914

Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01Vat3P5EcKjHcRUzSCTtyyu

* refactor: always store a parsed PyJWKSet in the JWK Set cache

The previous commit made `get_jwk_set()` tolerate either a `PyJWKSet` or
a `dict` coming back from the cache, which fixed #914 but left the cache
itself holding whichever type the caller happened to put in.

Normalize on write instead: `JWKSetCache.put()` accepts a `PyJWKSet` or
the raw JWKS payload and always stores it parsed, so `get()` is typed and
behaves as `Optional[PyJWKSet]` with no union leaking to callers. Cache
hits no longer re-parse (and re-load through `cryptography`) every key,
at the cost of returning one shared `PyJWKSet` instance while it stays
cached.

Parsing the payload on write hid the endpoint-response check behind a
vaguer "Invalid JWK Set value", so that check moves into `fetch_data()`,
next to the response it is actually about. Callers going through
`get_jwk_set()` see the same error as before; a direct `fetch_data()`
call now raises instead of returning a non-object payload.

Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01Vat3P5EcKjHcRUzSCTtyyu

* docs: link PR #1208 from the changelog entries

Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01Vat3P5EcKjHcRUzSCTtyyu

* test: cover clearing the JWK Set cache with put(None)

Restructuring `put()` made codecov count its cache-clearing branch as a
changed line, and it had no test. Clearing the cache is part of the
public behavior, so cover it rather than exempt it.

Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01Vat3P5EcKjHcRUzSCTtyyu

* fix: cache the key set get_jwk_set() actually returns

`fetch_data()` caches the payload it received from the endpoint, but a
subclass may filter or transform that payload before returning it. Since
`put()` now parses on write, the cache kept a snapshot taken before the
subclass ran, and the next cache hit served the pre-transform key set —
a key the subclass had removed came back.

On master this happened to work for an override that mutates the dict in
place, because the cache held a reference to that same dict; an override
returning a new dict was already broken. Cache the value `get_jwk_set()`
is about to return instead, which fixes both.

Also makes the returned set and the cached set the same object on the
fetch path, so repeated calls are identical rather than merely equal.

Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01Vat3P5EcKjHcRUzSCTtyyu

* fix: treat malformed JWK Set members as unusable keys

`PyJWKSet` skips keys it cannot use and raises `PyJWKSetError` when none
remain, but two malformed inputs escaped that contract with exceptions
that are not `PyJWTError`, so callers catching PyJWT's own exceptions saw
an uncaught crash instead:

- a member that is not a JSON object (`{"keys": [null]}`) reached
  `PyJWK.__init__` and raised `AttributeError`
- a key whose components have the wrong type
  (`{"kty": "RSA", "n": 1, "e": "AQAB"}`) raised `TypeError` out of
  `Algorithm.from_jwk`, which the surrounding handler only caught for
  `ValueError`

Both are reachable from `PyJWKClient`, whose payload comes straight from
a JWKS endpoint. Skip non-object members like any other unusable key, and
widen the `from_jwk` handler to `TypeError` so a bad component type
becomes `InvalidKeyError`. A single bad entry no longer fails an
otherwise usable JWK Set, and a set with nothing usable left raises
`PyJWKSetError`.

subject: fix: close HTTPError to prevent ResourceWarning on Python 3.14 (#1133)
problem_statement:
fix: close HTTPError to prevent ResourceWarning on Python 3.14 (#1133)

* fix: close HTTPError response to prevent ResourceWarning on Python 3.14

On Python 3.14, urllib.error.HTTPError objects that are not explicitly
closed produce a ResourceWarning during garbage collection. Since
HTTPError is both a URLError subclass and a response-like object
(inheriting from tempfile._TemporaryFileWrapper via addinfourl), it
must be closed to release the underlying resource.

This adds an explicit e.close() call in the except handler of
PyJWKClient.fetch_data() when the caught exception is an HTTPError.

Fixes #1128

* [pre-commit.ci] auto fixes from pre-commit.com hooks

for more information, see https://pre-commit.ci

* fix: use BytesIO for HTTPError fp in test to fix Python 3.9 compatibility

On Python 3.9, HTTPError(fp=None).close() triggers a KeyError in
tempfile.SpooledTemporaryFile.__getattr__ because the internal 'file'
dict key doesn't exist. Using io.BytesIO(b"") as the fp argument
provides a valid file-like object that can be closed on all Python
versions.

Also adds CHANGELOG.rst entry for the HTTPError close fix.

* fix: fall back to ASCII for the parallel banner and status header

problem_statement:
fix: keep an empty inner @parametrize from being dropped when stacked (#1138)

update_param_specs used `if not param_specs` to detect "no previous
@parametrize", but an inner `@parametrize("a", [])` sets the attribute to
an empty list, not None. `not []` is also true, so the empty dimension
was silently discarded instead of making the Cartesian product empty.

Stacking an empty parametrize under a non-empty one therefore produced
sessions missing the `a` argument (they raise TypeError at run time),
while the same empty parametrize on top correctly yields no sessions.
nox documents an empty parametrize as a do-nothing placeholder, so

subject: fix: correct python_versions() minimum for major-only and multiple lower bounds (#1127)
problem_statement:
fix: correct python_versions() minimum for major-only and multiple lower bounds (#1127)

* fix: correct python_versions() minimum for major-only and multiple lower bounds

nox.project.python_versions(pyproject, max_version=...) parsed the lower
bound from requires-python by looping over the SpecifierSet and breaking on
the first lower-bound specifier it saw, reading its minor version with
`spec.version.split(".")[1]`. This had two bugs:

1. Crash on a major-only version. A valid requires-python of ">=3" (which
   PEP 440 defines as equivalent to ">=3.0") has no minor component, so
   `"3".split(".")[1]` raised a cryptic `IndexError: list index out of range`
   from this public helper.

2. Wrong result with multiple lower bounds. For ">=3.8,>=3.10" the effective
   minimum is 3.10, but breaking on the first lower-bound specifier returned
   3.8 as the minimum, so the result claimed support for 3.8 and 3.9 which the
   metadata explicitly excludes. The output could even depend on specifier
   iteration order.

Fix: collect every lower-bound (">", ">=", "~=") specifier's minor version,
treating a major-only version as minor 0, and use the maximum as the
effective minimum. If there is no lower-bound specifier at all, the existing
ValueError is still raised.

Added regression tests for the major-only and multiple-lower-bound cases.

subject: perf: cache session-name normalization, uv detection, interpreter discovery, and metadata reads (#1113)
problem_statement:
perf: cache session-name normalization, uv detection, interpreter discovery, and metadata reads (#1113)

* perf: cache session-name normalization in manifest filtering

_normalize_arg runs ast.parse + ast.dump (~10us) for every
(specified name x queued session x signature) pair, plus the
missing-session check. Cache it with functools.cache (pure function
of a string) and hoist the needle normalization out of the signature
loop. A 600-session noxfile with 20 -s selections drops from ~400ms
to ~10ms in filter_by_name.

Assisted-by: ClaudeCode:claude-fable-5

* perf: detect uv lazily instead of at import time

find_uv() spawns 'uv self version' (two subprocesses for uv<0.7) at
module import, so every nox invocation -- including --version and
--list, and every 'import nox' in a noxfile -- paid that cost even
when uv was never used.

HAS_UV, UV, UV_VERSION, and OPTIONAL_VENVS (which depends on HAS_UV)
are now served by a module-level __getattr__ (PEP 562) and find_uv()
is cached. allowed_globals becomes a property so the uv path is read
at use time rather than captured at class creation; internal readers
go through the module attributes so monkeypatching them in tests (and
noxfiles) keeps working. A test asserts that importing nox.virtualenv
spawns no subprocess.

Assisted-by: ClaudeCode:claude-fable-5

* perf: cache interpreter discovery across sessions

Each session constructs a fresh VirtualEnv, so the per-instance
_resolved cache never helps across sessions: N sessions on the same
interpreter repeat the PATH lookup, and on Windows a PATH miss spawns
'py -X.Y -c ...' (~50-100 ms) per session. Cache the module-level
_find_python with functools.cache instead. Tests clear the cache
around each test since they monkeypatch PATH and _PLATFORM.

Assisted-by: ClaudeCode:claude-fable-5

* perf: avoid re-reading metadata for repeated requirements

get_dependencies() called importlib.metadata.metadata() (a dist-info
scan) on every visit and re-walked shared dependencies reachable
through multiple extras; this runs at startup whenever the noxfile
has a PEP 723 script block. Track visited (canonical name, extras)
pairs so each package's metadata is read and expanded once. Repeated
requirements are still yielded so every specifier is checked, and the
seen-set also terminates dependency-graph cycles, which previously
recursed forever.

Assisted-by: ClaudeCode:claude-fable-5

* test: keep uv detection out of mocked shutil.which windows

The autouse fixture cleared find_uv's cache around every test, so the
first lazy HAS_UV access inside a test that mocks shutil.which or
subprocess.run re-ran uv detection against the mocks, leaking a stray
which('uv') call into assert_called_once_with checks (order-dependent
under xdist).

Warm find_uv() once per session/worker before any mocking instead, and
keep per-test cache clearing only for _find_python. test_find_uv now
calls find_uv.__wrapped__ so it still exercises the real detection
logic under its mocks without touching the warmed cache.

Assisted-by: ClaudeCode:claude-fable-5

subject: fix: script-mode pip resolution on Windows and --download-python fallback (#1110)
problem_statement:
fix: script-mode pip resolution on Windows and --download-python fallback (#1110)

Two fixes for PEP 723 script mode in run_script_mode/_main:

- Resolve pip via shutil.which() against the script environment's PATH
  before invoking it. On Windows, CreateProcess searches the parent
  process's PATH rather than the child env's, so the bare "pip" command
  could resolve to an outer pip (installing script dependencies into the
  wrong environment) or fail entirely. This matches the existing pattern
  used to locate the nox executable.

- Make --download-python (and NOX_DOWNLOAD_PYTHON) work as a fallback in
  script mode. The TOML lookup used a truthy default of "auto", which
  made the 'or args.download_python' fallback unreachable. Precedence is
  now: NOX_SCRIPT_DOWNLOAD_PYTHON > tool.nox.script-download-python >
  --download-python/NOX_DOWNLOAD_PYTHON > "auto".

subject: fix: don't crash when a parametrized session has an empty parameter list (#1109)
problem_statement:
fix: don't crash when a parametrized session has an empty parameter list (#1109)

A noxfile with a zero-parameter parametrize, e.g.

    @nox.session
    @nox.parametrize("x", [])
    def empty(session, x): ...

made every nox invocation (including `nox -l`) fail with
"Error while resolving session dependencies." The placeholder session
created for an empty parametrize has no signatures, so it never entered
the dependency graph built from `all_sessions_by_signature`, and the
resolver raised a raw KeyError for the queued session.

Include any queued sessions missing from the dependency graph so that
the placeholder is resolved normally again: it shows up in listings and
reports as skipped ("This session had no parameters available.") while
other sessions run, matching the behavior of nox 2024.4.15.

Assisted-by: ClaudeCode:claude-fable-5

subject: fix: hash fully non-ASCII session names instead of returning the envdir (#1108)
problem_statement:
fix: hash fully non-ASCII session names instead of returning the envdir (#1108)

A session name with no ASCII word characters (e.g. "测试") was reduced
to the empty string by NFKD normalization, ascii-ignore encoding, and
the regex substitutions in _normalize_path. The resulting virtualenv
location was the envdir itself (e.g. .nox/), so two such sessions
silently shared one environment, and VirtualEnv._clean_location() would
shutil.rmtree() the entire envdir, deleting every other session's venv.

When the normalized name comes out empty, fall back to the same sha1
hash used for over-long names, hashing the original (UTF-8) name so the
result is a stable, unique subdirectory of envdir.

subject: Fix `1 * unit` skipping auto_reduce_dimensions and autoconvert_to_preferred (#2419)
problem_statement:
Fix `1 * unit` skipping auto_reduce_dimensions and autoconvert_to_preferred (#2419)

* Fix `1 * unit` skipping auto_reduce_dimensions and autoconvert_to_preferred

`PlainUnit.__mul__` shortcuts a magnitude of 1 and returns the Quantity
directly, because non-multiplicative units such as degC cannot go through
the multiplication below it. Every other magnitude goes through
`PlainQuantity._mul_div`, which is wrapped in `ireduce_dimensions`, so the
two disagreed:

    >>> u = pint.UnitRegistry(auto_reduce_dimensions=True)
    >>> 1 * u.deg
    <Quantity(1, 'degree')>
    >>> 2 * u.deg
    <Quantity(0.034906585, 'dimensionless')>

The same split applied to `autoconvert_to_preferred`: `1 * u.km` kept
kilometre while `2 * u.km` converted to metre. The shortcut predates both
settings, so this was never a deliberate exemption.

Keep the shortcut, since offset units still depend on it, and apply the
same two conversions `ireduce_dimensions` applies on the other path.

Closes #2403

subject: Convert the units of the numpy 2.1 clip min/max keywords (#2434)
problem_statement:
Convert the units of the numpy 2.1 clip min/max keywords (#2434)

* Convert the units of the numpy 2.1 clip min/max keywords

numpy 2.1 added `min` and `max` as array-API compatible spellings of
`a_min`/`a_max`, documented as usable in place of them. The entry in
`numpy_func.py` only lists `a_min`/`a_max`, so with the new spellings the
bounds keep their Quantity and `implementation` calls back into
`np.clip` with them unconverted. numpy redispatches, `a` is no longer a
Quantity, `unwrap_and_wrap_consistent_units` finds nothing to convert
and returns the input unchanged, and the cycle repeats until
`RecursionError`.

Measured on numpy 2.5.3, before this change:

    np.clip(q, min=150 * ureg.cm)   -> RecursionError
    np.clip(q, min=Quantity(1, "J")) -> RecursionError
    np.clip(q, min=2)                -> [[2, 2], [3, 4]] meter

So a Quantity bound crashes, including the case that owed a
`DimensionalityError`, and a bare number is silently taken to be in the
input's units. The `Quantity.clip` method already does the right thing
for all three, and `test_clip` asserts that contract for `clip(ureg.J)`
and `clip(1)`.

Listing both spellings makes the function agree with the method.

subject: Fix @alias crashing on prefixed units with a bare KeyError (#2329)
problem_statement:
Fix @alias crashing on prefixed units with a bare KeyError (#2329)

* Fix @alias crashing on prefixed units with a bare KeyError

Aliasing a prefixed unit -- e.g. `@alias millimeter = DUT_MM` or
`@alias meV = my_energy` -- raised an unhandled `KeyError` from a
public API.

Root cause: `_add_alias` looked the target up with `self._units[definition.name]`,
but prefixed units (millimeter = milli + meter, meV = milli + eV) are
created lazily by `get_name`/`parse_unit_name` and are not present in
`self._units` until first resolved. On a fresh registry only the base
unit (`meter`) exists, so the raw dict lookup raised `KeyError` for the
prefixed spelling.

Fix: resolve the target through `self.get_name(...)` before the lookup,
mirroring how the rest of the registry resolves unit names. This
materializes the prefixed `UnitDefinition` into `self._units` (exactly as
attribute/parse access already does) so the alias registers correctly,
and it turns the lookup of a genuinely unknown target into a proper
`UndefinedUnitError` instead of a bare `KeyError`.

Adds `test_alias_prefixed_unit` (fails with `KeyError: 'millimeter'`
before the fix) and updates the existing unknown-alias assertion in
`test_alias` to expect `UndefinedUnitError`.

Fixes #1076

Per keewis's review, _is_timedelta/_convert_timedelta moved into the
numpy facet to keep np.timedelta64-specific detection out of plain.
But that also pulled in the stdlib datetime.timedelta branch, so
PlainQuantity.__new__ ended up depending on a NumpyQuantity-only
method (only working because NumpyQuantity is unconditionally mixed
into the default Quantity class).

datetime.timedelta needs nothing numpy-related, so give PlainQuantity
its own _is_timedelta/_convert_timedelta handling it directly, and
have NumpyQuantity override both to add the np.timedelta64/duck-array
cases, delegating to super() for the plain datetime.timedelta case.

Also switch the __new__ call site from the unbound-style
cls._is_timedelta(cls, value) to a normal inst._is_timedelta(value)
call now that it's a real instance method on the class being
constructed.

* Fix Q_(quantity, units) crashing via _is_timedelta's duck-array check

CI failure (docs doctest job): Q_(length, 'cm') raised AttributeError
when length was itself a Quantity, e.g.:

    AttributeError: Neither Quantity object nor its magnitude (30)
    has attribute 'dtype'

Root cause: is_duck_array_type (pint/compat.py) checks
hasattr(cls, "_magnitude")/hasattr(cls, "_units") on the *class* to
rule out Quantity types, but those attributes are only ever set on
*instances* (assigned in __new__), so hasattr on the bare class is

check happens later in __new__), gets a false positive, and crashes

problem_statement:
Respect format spec width/fill/alignment for quantities (#2355)

* Respect format spec width/fill/alignment for quantities (#1798)

A Python format spec applied to a Quantity, such as ``f"{q:20.1f}"`` or
``f"{q:>20}"``, did not honor the requested field width. The entire spec
(including the width/fill/alignment) was forwarded to ``format_magnitude``,
so the padding was applied to the magnitude alone and then the unit string
was appended, pushing the result past the requested width.

Root cause: in the plain-text formatters ``format_quantity`` passes the
magnitude spec straight through and only afterwards joins the unit, so any
width/fill/align in the spec pads the number instead of the final
"magnitude unit" string.

Fix: add ``split_magnitude_spec`` which separates the field portion
(fill/align/width) from the number portion (sign/precision/type/grouping).
The magnitude is formatted with the number portion, the unit is joined, and
the field portion is then applied to the whole string. Zero-padding (``0``)
and internal alignment (``=``) remain magnitude-only, matching Python's
numeric semantics. All four plain formatters (Default, Compact, Pretty, Raw)
are updated.

Support superscript decimal point and fraction slash in exponents (#2250) (#2330)

Unit strings could not use a superscript decimal point (`⋅`, U+22C5) or
fraction slash (`⸍`, U+2E0D) in exponents, so `gr⁰⋅³³³` and `gr¹⸍³`
raised UndefinedUnitError even though ordinary superscripts (`gr²`) worked.

Map `⋅` to `.` and `⸍` to `/` and extend the superscript exponent regex
to accept them; the existing `**(...)` wrapping keeps the fraction correctly
parenthesized (`gr¹⸍³` -> `gr**(1/3)`). The multiplication interpunct `·`
(U+00B7) is a distinct character and is unaffected. Adds tests.

subject: Fix KeyError('') when dimensionless is referenced by name (#2351)
problem_statement:
Fix KeyError('') when dimensionless is referenced by name (#2351)

* Fix KeyError('') when dimensionless is referenced by name

`get_name("dimensionless")` returns "" (the canonical dimensionless name),
which is not a key in `self._units`. `_get_dimensionality_recurse` and
`_get_root_units_recurse` indexed `self._units[self.get_name(key)]`
directly, so referencing `dimensionless` by name raised `KeyError('')`.

This happened both when a user passed the name directly
(`get_dimensionality("dimensionless")`, `Quantity(5, "dimensionless")
.check("dimensionless")`) and when the name was stored in a unit's
reference (a unit defined via `... * dimensionless`).

`dimensionless` is the identity: it contributes nothing to a
dimensionality and has no root units. Skip it in both loops, so a unit
like `frac = 0.01 * dimensionless` behaves identically to `frac = 0.01`.

Closes #1513
Closes #1994


* Simplify empty-name guard and drop restated comment

Use an explicit == "" comparison, matching get_name's str return
type, and drop the comment since the check now says what it means.

subject: Fix offset (affine) unit conversion of Decimal magnitudes (#2305) (#2318)
problem_statement:
Fix offset (affine) unit conversion of Decimal magnitudes (#2305) (#2318)

* Fix offset conversion of Decimal magnitudes (#2305)

OffsetConverter.to_reference/from_reference combined the magnitude with the
float scale and offset directly, so converting a Decimal magnitude across an
affine unit (e.g. degC -> K) raised TypeError because Decimal does not support
arithmetic with float. Coerce the scale/offset to a type compatible with the
magnitude before the arithmetic: promote to Decimal for a Decimal magnitude and
demote a Decimal scale/offset to float otherwise. This also fixes the mirror
case of a float magnitude in a non_int_type=Decimal registry.

* Move scalar type-coercion logic to shared coerce_scalar() in compat

The same Decimal/Fraction-vs-float coercion was duplicated in two places:
plain/registry.py (for multiplicative conversions) and a private
_matching_scalar in nonmultiplicative/definitions.py (for affine
conversions). Consolidate into coerce_scalar() in pint/compat.py so
the logic lives once and is testable in isolation.

The new helper also fixes a subtle difference: the original
_matching_scalar demoted any Decimal scalar to float for non-Decimal
values (including int), but int OP Decimal works fine. coerce_scalar
narrows the demotion to float values only, preserving the Decimal type
through int-magnitude conversions in a Decimal registry.


* Fix comment wording: promote -> coerce in OffsetConverter

subject: 🐛 FIX: IndexError in html_block/heading terminator rules at EOF (#416)
problem_statement:
🐛 FIX: IndexError in html_block/heading terminator rules at EOF (#416)

## Summary
Fixes #415. Input that ends on a blockquote marker while a table is open
inside that quote raises `IndexError: string index out of range`:

```python
from markdown_it import MarkdownIt

# html_block.py — raises IndexError
MarkdownIt().enable("table").parse("> | a | b |\n> |---|---|\n>")

# heading.py — same input, raises once html_block is out of the way
MarkdownIt("commonmark", {"html": False}).enable("table").parse("> | a | b |\n> |---|---|\n>")
```

## Root cause
With `table` enabled, `html_block` and `heading` run as **terminator
rules** on the empty final line that a trailing `>` produces. There,
`pos = state.bMarks[startLine] + state.tShift[startLine]` equals
`len(state.src)`, and both rules index `state.src[pos]` without guarding
that boundary:

- `html_block.py`: `if state.src[pos] != "<":`
- `heading.py`: `ch = state.src[pos]` — its `pos >= maximum` check is on
the *next* line, after the index

In markdown-it (JS) the equivalent `state.src.charCodeAt(pos)` returns
`NaN` out of range instead of raising — the port hazard tracked in #190.

## Fix
Sibling terminator rules already defend against exactly this — `hr.py`
and `blockquote.py` wrap the same index access in `try: ... except
IndexError: return False` (added for #185 / #204). `html_block.py` and
`heading.py` were missed. This applies the same established guard to
both.

`html_block` runs before `heading`, so it shadows it (disabling `html`
moves the traceback to `heading` rather than fixing it) — hence both
rules need the guard, and there is a regression test for each path.

## Tests
Added two regression tests in `tests/test_fuzzer.py` (the existing home
for crash-regression cases), one per crash path — asserting the input
renders without raising.

## Note on local verification
I verified the guard logic in isolation (the old expression raises
`IndexError` when `pos == len(src)`; the guarded version returns
`False`, i.e. the rule declines, with identical behavior for in-range
characters — matching how `hr.py`/`blockquote.py` already behave). I was
not able to run the full pytest suite locally (my environment's Python
predates this package's minimum), so I'd appreciate CI confirming the
two new tests pass and that the rendered output for that input is
sensible. Happy to adjust the tests to assert exact rendered HTML if
you'd prefer that over "does not raise".

subject: ✨ Add `make_fence_rule()` factory for configurable fence markers (#394)
problem_statement:
✨ Add `make_fence_rule()` factory for configurable fence markers (#394)

Adds a `make_fence_rule()` factory function that generates fence parsing
rules with configurable options, enabling reuse of the fence logic for
custom marker characters (e.g. `:` for colon fences) without code
duplication.

## Motivation

The `colon_fence` plugin in `mdit-py-plugins` duplicates nearly all of
the fence parsing logic, differing only in the marker character (`:` vs
`` ` ``/`~`), token type, and info-string restrictions. This makes
maintenance harder and prevents features like exact-match closing from
being shared.

## Changes

- **New `make_fence_rule()` factory** in fence.py with parameters:
- `markers`: tuple of valid fence marker characters (default `("~",
"\`")`)
  - `token_type`: token type name to emit (default `"fence"`)
- `exact_match`: when `True`, closing fence must have **exactly** the
same marker count as the opener (default `False`). This enables nested
fences (e.g. `::::` wrapping `:::`).
- `disallow_marker_in_info`: marker characters that reject the fence if
found in the info string (default `("\`",)` per CommonMark)
  - `min_markers`: minimum marker count to form a fence (default `3`)

- **`fence` remains a module-level export**: `fence = make_fence_rule()`
— fully backwards compatible, identical behavior to the previous
implementation.

- **Exported from `markdown_it.rules_block`** — added `make_fence_rule`
to `__all__`.

## Usage

```python
from markdown_it import MarkdownIt
from markdown_it.rules_block.fence import make_fence_rule

# Colon fence (replaces mdit-py-plugins/colon_fence duplicated logic)
md = MarkdownIt()
md.block.ruler.before("fence", "colon_fence",
    make_fence_rule(markers=(":",), token_type="colon_fence", disallow_marker_in_info=()))

# Override standard fence with exact-match closing (for MyST nested directives)
md.block.ruler.at("fence", make_fence_rule(exact_match=True))

# Combine: all markers with exact matching
md.block.ruler.at("fence", make_fence_rule(
    markers=("~", "`", ":"), exact_match=True))
```

## Performance

No regression by design — configuration is captured in the closure at
rule-creation time (no runtime dict lookups or extra branches in the hot
path). The `closing_matcher` callable is resolved once at factory time.

## Tests

21 new tests covering:
- Colon-fence-like marker behavior
- Exact-match closing (nesting patterns)
- `ruler.at()` override of standard fence
- `min_markers` customization
- `disallow_marker_in_info` variations

Full existing test suite (981 tests) passes unchanged.

subject: ✨Allow plugins to register inline terminator characters (#391)
problem_statement:
✨Allow plugins to register inline terminator characters (#391)

The inline `text` rule used a hardcoded, unexpandable set of terminator
characters, forcing plugins that need to trigger on non-terminator
characters (e.g. `w` for GFM `www.` autolinks) to resort to core-rule
post-processing workarounds.

## Changes

- **`parser_inline.py`**: Moves the terminator set onto `ParserInline`
as `_terminator_chars` (a `set[str]` seeded from `_DEFAULT_TERMINATORS`)
with a pre-compiled `terminator_re: re.Pattern[str]` attribute. Exposes
`add_terminator_char(ch)` to extend the set; the regex is rebuilt
eagerly only when a genuinely new character is added, keeping zero
per-call overhead in the hot path.

- **`rules_inline/text.py`**: Drops the module-level `_TerminatorChars`
set and `@functools.cache`-decorated factory. The `text` rule now reads
`state.md.inline.terminator_re` directly.

- **`docs/contributing.md`**: Updates the "Why is my inline rule not
executed?" FAQ to document the new API.

## Usage

```python
def gfm_autolink_plugin(md: MarkdownIt) -> None:
    md.inline.add_terminator_char("w")
    md.inline.ruler.push("gfm_autolink_www", _www_rule)
```

Fully backward-compatible — the default terminator set is unchanged.

subject: 👌 Fix quadratic complexity in `fragments_join` / `text_join` (#389)
problem_statement:
👌 Fix quadratic complexity in `fragments_join` / `text_join` (#389)

Optimize adjacent-token joining in both inline cleanup stages by
replacing repeated pairwise string concatenation with a single
`"".join(...)` over each contiguous run.

## Details

- `fragments_join` merges adjacent `text` tokens left behind after
emphasis/strikethrough post-processing and recalculates token levels
- `text_join` converts `text_special` tokens to `text` and performs the
final adjacent-text merge in the inline token stream

Both rules previously rebuilt growing strings incrementally, which can
become quadratic for long runs.

## Why

Tested on an adversarial ~190 KB document with ~30k intraword
underscores on a single line. With `tracemalloc` running:

|           | render time | peak Python alloc |
|-----------|-------------|-------------------|
| before    | 2.2s        | 4476 MB           |
| after     | 0.6s        | 23 MB             |

It's not just a contrived attack input - this kind of thing also shows
up naturally in Markdown produced by OCR pipelines, where tables of
identifiers / references can easily contain very long runs of
underscores or other delimiter characters.

## Tests

Added focused tests for both rules:

- `fragments_join`: verifies raw adjacent text fragments remain when
both join stages are disabled, and that `fragments_join` alone collapses
them when `text_join` is disabled
- `text_join`: verifies escaped characters remain as multiple
`text_special` tokens when `text_join` is disabled, and are converted
and merged into a single `text` token when enabled

## Result

No behavioral change in parser output, with less unnecessary work when
joining long runs of adjacent tokens.

subject: When a parse action returns a non-ParseResults, non-list value
problem_statement:
When a parse action returns a non-ParseResults, non-list value
(e.g. a tuple, set, or defaultdict), the named result was being
set to only the first element (tokens[0]) instead of the full
return value. This happened because the value was passed directly
to ParseResults(), which indexes into it with 'toklist[0]' for
the named result.

Fix: wrap non-list, non-ParseResults return values in [tokens]
before constructing the ParseResults, so toklist[0] returns the
full value. Null values (empty tuple) are not wrapped because
ParseResults._null_values expects them directly to clear the
result. Lists preserve their existing behavior of spreading
elements as the token list.

Partially fixes #401

subject: Fix match_previous_expr to match nested and repeated expressions (#653)
problem_statement:
Fix match_previous_expr to match nested and repeated expressions (#653)

copy_token_to_repeater added a new guard parse action to the repeated
expression on every match of the leading expression, and never removed
one. After N matches all N guards ran on each attempt to match, so at
most one could succeed. A second pair anywhere in the input failed, and
once a parse had failed the expression kept rejecting valid input.

Keep the pending matches on a stack instead, and register the guard once
at construction, so an inner match pairs with the nearest enclosing
match. Entries recorded at or after the current location are dropped, so
matches left behind by a backtracked branch cannot be paired.

Issue #560

subject: Fix RecursionError for bounded repetition with large upper bound (issue #332) (#652)
problem_statement:
Fix RecursionError for bounded repetition with large upper bound (issue #332) (#652)

* Fix RecursionError for bounded repetition with large upper bound (issue #332)

Build the optional tail of `expr * (m, n)` as a flat list of independent
`Optional` expressions instead of a deeply nested `Optional(self + ...)`
chain. The nested form recursed `optElements` levels deep, raising
RecursionError for large upper bounds such as `expr[..., 1000]`.

Fixes #332.

* Preserve early-exit in bounded repetition (issue #332)

Replace the flat And([Opt(self)] * optElements) tail with a bounded
ZeroOrMore(self, max=optElements). The flat list always attempted self for
every remaining slot in the upper bound, losing the original recursive
form's early-exit behavior (ptmcg's review on PR #652). The bounded loop
is flat (no RecursionError at large upper bounds) and still stops at the
first non-match, so construction, parsing, and early-exit all hold.

- Add optional max bound to _MultipleMatch/ZeroOrMore
- Add testBoundedRepetitionLargeUpperBoundEarlyExit regression test

* Added validation for max parameter, must be > 0; added unit tests for added max parameter

subject: Copy the occurrence lists when renumbering, not when copying
problem_statement:
Copy the occurrence lists when renumbering, not when copying

Copying them in copy() put the cost on the parse path: with packrat or
left-recursion enabled, copy() runs on every cache store and every cache hit,
and the dict comprehension cost ~90ns even when there are no results names at
all.

Only __delitem__ and insert renumber the recorded offsets, so let copy() keep
sharing the lists and have those two renumber a private copy instead.
__setitem__ and __iadd__ already build new lists.

Measured, 200k iterations each, best of five:

  copy() with 3 results names   311 -> 637 -> 323 ns
  copy() with no results names  277 -> 365 -> 276 ns
  insert()                     1192 -> 1173 -> 1548 ns
  del r[0]                     1626 -> 1581 -> 2067 ns

(unpatched -> copying in copy() -> copying when renumbering)

subject: Give ParseResults.copy() its own results-name bookkeeping
problem_statement:
Give ParseResults.copy() its own results-name bookkeeping

copy() copies the token list, but `{**self._tokdict}` copies only the outer
dict -- the per-name lists of _ParseResultsWithOffset are shared with the
original. insert() and __delitem__() renumber those offsets by assigning into
the list in place, so mutating a copy writes straight into the original's
bookkeeping:

    expr = pp.Word(pp.nums) + pp.Word(pp.nums)("b")

    r = expr.parse_string("1 2")
    del r[0]
    r.get_name()          # 'b'

    r = expr.parse_string("1 2")
    c = r.copy()
    c.insert(0, "X")      # touches the copy...
    del r[0]
    r.get_name()          # None -- the original's 'b' offset was renumbered

deepcopy() is unaffected: it rebuilds _tokdict with fresh lists.

The documented contract is that the contained items are shared -- _toklist is
already copied, so the offset table is structure, not content. Copy the
occurrence lists as well. copy() is not called during parsing, and the lists
are almost always a single element.

subject: Preserve whitespace in QuotedString multi-char delimiters (fixes #492)
problem_statement:
Preserve whitespace in QuotedString multi-char delimiters (fixes #492)

QuotedString.__init__ called quote_char.strip() (and end_quote_char.strip())
to reject empty/whitespace-only delimiters. But strip() also removed leading
or trailing whitespace that is a legitimate part of a multi-character
delimiter. For example QuotedString("\n;", multiline=True) had its quote_char
silently collapsed to ";", so the newline in the delimiter was ignored and
matching started/ended at the wrong positions.

Fix: validate with `not quote_char.strip()` to keep rejecting empty or
all-whitespace delimiters, but assign the original, unstripped value so
embedded whitespace in a valid delimiter is preserved. Same for end_quote_char.

Added a regression test covering the reported cases and confirming that empty
and all-whitespace quote chars are still rejected.

subject: Carry a rounded-up fractional second in as_datetime instead of overflowing
problem_statement:
Carry a rounded-up fractional second in as_datetime instead of overflowing

pyparsing_common.as_datetime scaled the fractional seconds with
round((second % 1) * 1_000_000) and passed the result straight to
datetime's microsecond argument. A fractional value that rounds up to a
full second (e.g. "2021-06-15T12:30:59.9999995", or the trailing digits of
a nanosecond-precision timestamp) produces exactly 1_000_000, which is
outside datetime's 0..999999 range, so the constructor raised ValueError
and as_datetime re-wrapped it as "Invalid date/time" for input whose date
and time fields are all valid.

Add the rounded microseconds via timedelta so the value carries into the
next second. Sub-microsecond and <=6-digit fractions are unchanged
(0.45 -> 450000, 0.999999 -> 999999), and int(second) still rejects a
literal "60" leap second as before.

fix: deepcopy results names referencing nested ParseResults

ParseResults.deepcopy() only deep-copied the token list; the results-name

problem_statement:
Fix Located capturing leading whitespace in its location (#621)

Located adopts callPreparse from the wrapped expression. When that
expression delegates whitespace skipping to its sub-expressions (such as
MatchFirst or And, whose callPreparse is False), Located does not
pre-parse it, so parseImpl captured start on the leading whitespace and
locn_start (and the located span) wrongly included that whitespace.

marks the real start of the match. Expressions modified with
leave_whitespace() still keep their leading whitespace.

Closes #781, #783

Refs https://github.com/simonw/sqlite-utils/issues/769#issuecomment-4900618685

* Fix rowid pk and last_rowid regressions in insert/upsert

Two behaviour regressions in the 4.0 insert/upsert rewrite broke callers
(notably Datasette's write API) that operate on tables without an explicit
primary key. Both are fixed here with regression tests.

1. rowid (and its aliases _rowid_/oid) were rejected as a primary key.
   Table.pks already reports ["rowid"] for a rowid table, but the new pk
   validation raised InvalidColumns because rowid is not listed among the
   table's columns, and the insert success path then raised KeyError when
   looking up the pk value. rowid aliases are now accepted for rowid tables
   and resolve directly to the rowid.

2. An ignored insert (INSERT OR IGNORE that matched an existing row) no
   longer populated last_rowid, and only set last_pk when an explicit pk=
   was passed. It now locates the existing conflicting row by its primary
   key values and reports that row's rowid and pk, rather than relying on
   the connection's last inserted rowid.

Add a shared ROWID_ALIASES constant for the rowid alias names.

* Fix transform() corrupting TRUE/FALSE/NULL column defaults

quote_default_value() passed keyword-literal defaults (TRUE, FALSE, NULL)
through self.quote(), wrapping them in quotes. So transform() rebuilt a
column declared "INTEGER DEFAULT TRUE" as "INTEGER DEFAULT 'TRUE'", and a

subject: Replace SQL prefix matching with a first-token scanner
problem_statement:
Replace SQL prefix matching with a first-token scanner

query() and execute() classified statements using
sql.lstrip().upper().startswith(...), which a leading SQL comment
defeated: db.query('/* c */ COMMIT') inside db.atomic() committed
the caller's transaction and masked the ValueError with a 'no such
savepoint' error, comment-prefixed PRAGMAs ran inside the savepoint
guard where journal mode changes are refused, and a comment-prefixed
BEGIN passed to db.execute() was instantly auto-committed.

The new _first_keyword() helper skips leading whitespace and -- or
/* */ comments - the only things SQLite's tokenizer allows before
the first token - and returns that token for exact comparison, so
keyword detection now matches what SQLite itself will see.

subject: Improve db.query() error handling and transaction safety
problem_statement:
Improve db.query() error handling and transaction safety 

db.query() rejected statements roll back, RETURNING commits immediately.

Fixes two transaction bugs in db.query():

- A non-row-returning statement such as an UPDATE was executed and
  auto-committed by execute() before the ValueError was raised, so the
  write took effect despite being rejected. query() now runs the
  statement inside a savepoint and rolls it back before raising, so a
  rejected statement has no effect on the database - in every
  connection mode, including autocommit=True.

- INSERT ... RETURNING only committed once the returned generator was
  fully exhausted, so calling query() without iterating - or partially
  iterating with next() - left the transaction open and the write could
  be rolled back on close. The write is now completed and committed at
  call time, as the documentation already promised. Plain SELECTs are
  still fetched lazily.

Transaction control statements, VACUUM, ATTACH and DETACH never return
rows, so query() now rejects them without executing them. PRAGMA
statements skip the savepoint guard because some of them - such as
pragma journal_mode=wal - refuse to run inside a transaction.

fix(pendulum_dt): stop DateTime defaulting a naive input to UTC (#427)

DateTime._validate called pendulum.DateTime.instance(value) at all three
exit paths (existing-instance passthrough, the core-schema handler
result, and the parse() fallback) with no tz argument, and
instance()'s own default is tz='UTC'. That default only applies when
the input is naive (tz = dt.tzinfo or tz), so every naive input silently
came back UTC-aware instead of staying naive, unlike pydantic's stdlib
datetime.

The parse() fallback path needed its own tz=None too: pendulum.parse()
defaults a naive string to UTC before DateTime.instance ever sees the
result, so fixing instance() alone left that path unchanged.

Pass tz=None at all three sites. For an already-aware value this is a
no-op (dt.tzinfo takes precedence over the tz argument), so the fix for
#188 (aware inputs keep their own offset) is unaffected.

fix: reject MAC address octets with a sign or whitespace (#424)

MacAddress.validate_mac_address parsed each octet with int(part, 16),
which also accepts a leading +/- sign and surrounding whitespace. As a
result strings like -a:-b:-c:-d:-e:-f, +a:+b:+c:+d:+e:+f and
" a: b: c: d: e: f" were accepted, with the sign/whitespace variants
silently normalized into a valid-looking MAC the caller never supplied.

Require both characters of each octet to be hex digits before the int()
conversion so malformed octets raise the mac_address_format error like
other invalid input.

subject: fix(isin, isbn, iban): reject non-ASCII digits (#410)
problem_statement:
fix(isin, isbn, iban): reject non-ASCII digits (#410)

str.isdigit()/isalnum() accept non-ASCII numerals (Arabic-Indic, fullwidth,
etc.), and int('٥') == 5 keeps the checksum valid, so ISIN, ISBN and IBAN
each accepted 'validated' identifiers that contain non-ASCII characters and
violate their ISO standards -- e.g. ISIN('US037833100٥'), the ISBN-10 path
even emitting a converted ISBN-13 that still carries the non-ASCII char.

Guard each character check with str.isascii(), mirroring the fix already
applied to the sibling ABARoutingNumber in #403. Superscript digits (isdigit
True but int() raises) are covered too, so they no longer leak an int
conversion error. Legitimate ASCII identifiers, including ISBN-10 check
digit 'X', are unaffected.

fix(ulid, color): raise ValidationError for types float()/from_bytes reject (#409)

#312 widened `except ValueError` to `except (ValueError, TypeError)` in
color.py to fix #311 ("Unhandled validation error when parsing Color"),
because float() raises TypeError -- not ValueError -- for a value whose
*type* it cannot take at all. Two call sites with the identical construct
were not updated:

  Something(ulid=1.5)      -> TypeError: object of type 'float' has no len()
  Color((0, 0, 0, []))     -> TypeError: float() argument must be a string...

TypeError is not a subclass of ValueError, so neither except clause fires
and the error escapes validate_python raw.

- ulid.py:66     _validate_ulid is a wrap validator, so it sees the raw
                 value before the inner union_schema can reject it; the
                 else branch hands it to _ULID.from_bytes.
- color.py:391   parse_float_alpha's own docstring says it raises
                 PydanticCustomError "if the input value cannot be
                 successfully parsed as a float"; a list cannot be.

Same one-line widening as #312 in both, reusing each site's existing error.

subject: fix(isbn, iban, mac_address): raise ValidationError for non-string input (#408)
problem_statement:
fix(isbn, iban, mac_address): raise ValidationError for non-string input (#408)

ISBN, IBAN and MacAddress register `_validate` as a *before* validator, so
it runs ahead of `str_schema()` and receives the raw input. Each then calls a
str-only method on it -- `len()`, `.replace()`, `.encode()` -- so a non-string
leaks TypeError/AttributeError out of validation instead of raising
ValidationError:

    Book(isbn=9780306406157)     -> TypeError: object of type 'int' has no len()
    BankAccount(iban=12345)      -> AttributeError: 'int' object has no attribute 'replace'
    Network(mac_address=12345)   -> AttributeError: 'int' object has no attribute 'encode'

`except ValidationError` does not catch these.

DomainStr is the fourth before-validator and gets this right: it annotates the
input as `Any` and raises PydanticCustomError('domain_type', 'Value must be a
string'). These three annotate the input as `str` -- which the before-validator
cannot guarantee -- and omit the check. Apply DomainStr's pattern to each.

The after-validator types (ISIN, routing_number, payment, ...) are unaffected:
str_schema() rejects non-strings before their `_validate` runs. ISIN's
test_isin_requires_string already asserts this contract.

subject: fix(pendulum_dt): preserve Interval boundaries on JSON serialization (#407)
problem_statement:
fix(pendulum_dt): preserve Interval boundaries on JSON serialization (#407)

`Interval.__get_pydantic_core_schema__` wrapped the validator around a bare
`str_schema()` with no `serialization` schema. On JSON serialization pydantic-core
fell back to the duration path (an Interval subclasses Duration/timedelta), so
`model_dump_json()` emitted only the interval's length -- e.g. `"P1D"` -- dropping
the start/end boundaries, and the resulting string then failed to re-validate.
The round-trip both lost data and raised `ValidationError`.

Add a serializer that emits the `start/end` ISO form the validator already
accepts, mirroring the sibling `Duration` type's `plain_serializer_function_ser_schema`
(`when_used='json-unless-none'`). `model_dump_json()` now yields
`"2021-01-01T00:00:00+00:00/2021-01-02T00:00:00+00:00"`, which re-validates to an
equal Interval. Python-mode `model_dump()` is unchanged (it still returns the
Interval object, as before).

Add a parametrized JSON round-trip regression test; it was red before the fix
(the serialized `"P1D"` failed to re-validate) and is green after.

subject: fix(ulid): make ULID serializable to JSON (#406)
problem_statement:
fix(ulid): make ULID serializable to JSON (#406)

A ULID field cannot be serialized to JSON at all:

    class Something(BaseModel):
        ulid: ULID

    Something(ulid="01BTGNYV6HRNK8K8VKZASZCFPE").model_dump_json()
    PydanticSerializationError: Unable to serialize unknown type: <class 'ulid.ULID'>

The core schema only wires up validation. After validation the value is a
python-ulid ULID instance, and the union's leading is_instance_schema carries
no serializer, so pydantic has no way to render it.

The published schema says otherwise: test_json_schema already asserts that
mode="serialization" advertises integer/string/binary/uuid, so the schema
promises something the runtime cannot deliver.

Add a json serializer, matching the convention MongoObjectId already uses
(plain_serializer_function_ser_schema(..., when_used="json")). Python-mode
model_dump() still yields the ULID object, and the serialization json schema
is unchanged.

subject: fix(mongo_object_id): validate ObjectId when parsing from JSON (#405)
problem_statement:
fix(mongo_object_id): validate ObjectId when parsing from JSON (#405)

The JSON branch of the core schema only constrained the string length:

    json_schema=core_schema.str_schema(min_length=24, max_length=24)

while the Python branch also ran cls.validate, which checks ObjectId.is_valid.
A 24-character non-hex string was therefore accepted from JSON and left as a
plain str, so the same value behaved differently depending on the entry point:

    M(id="z" * 24)                              # ValidationError
    M.model_validate_json('{"id": "zzz…"}')     # accepted, id is a str

Share one schema between both branches, built with an after-validator over the
length-checked string. Using no_info_after_validator_function rather than a
chain keeps the underlying str_schema visible to the JSON Schema generator:
model_json_schema() is unchanged in both validation and serialization mode
(a chain_schema breaks serialization mode with invalid-for-json-schema).

test_get_pydantic_core_schema asserted json_schema['type'] == 'str', which is
exactly the shape of the bug -- it pinned the JSON branch to a bare length
check. Updated to assert the after-validator wrapping the str schema.

subject: fix(epoch): raise ValidationError for out-of-range timestamps (#404)
problem_statement:
fix(epoch): raise ValidationError for out-of-range timestamps (#404)

epoch.Integer / epoch.Number computed `EPOCH + timedelta(seconds=value)`
with no error handling. A timestamp past datetime.max (e.g. a JavaScript
millisecond epoch like 1721000000000 accidentally passed to a seconds
field) raises OverflowError, which is not a ValueError subclass, so
pydantic does not convert it — it escapes validate_python as a raw
exception instead of a ValidationError.

Catch the overflow and raise ValueError so pydantic surfaces it as a
ValidationError, which callers wrapping validation can handle normally.

subject: dictutils: preserve iterator values in addlist (#458)
problem_statement:
dictutils: preserve iterator values in addlist (#458)

addlist() traverses its argument twice: once to insert the keys into the
linked list, once to extend the backing values list. A one-shot iterator
is exhausted by the first pass, so the second added nothing and the OMD
was left internally inconsistent - keys() and repr() showed the values
while getlist() returned [] and get() raised IndexError.

An empty iterator was worse: the `if not v` guard is truthy for an
exhausted generator, so the key was recorded with no values and len()
disagreed with keys().

Materialize the argument once, before the guard. The docstring already
promises that "tuples and other sequences and iterables work"; the
doctest uses range(), which is re-iterable, which is why this went
unnoticed. urlutils carries a vendored copy of the method with the same
defect, so it gets the same fix.

subject: funcutils: forward target-keyword-only args as keywords in wraps invocations (#445)
problem_statement:
funcutils: forward target-keyword-only args as keywords in wraps invocations (#445)

wraps(g)(f) generates a shim with g's signature that calls f. When f
declares a parameter keyword-only that g accepts positionally, the
generated invocation passed it positionally and f raised TypeError
(#261). The defaulted flavor of this was fixed as a side effect of
the #343 keyword-forwarding work; the non-defaulted flavor (donor arg
positional and undefaulted) and the varargs flavor still broke.

get_invocation_str() now takes an optional 'target' -- the callable
the generated invocation will call -- and forwards any arg that
target only accepts as a keyword as name=name, overriding the
positional rules (including the varargs one: _call(a, *va, b=b) binds
correctly precisely because a target-kw-only name can never collide
with target's positionals). update_wrapper passes wrapper as the
target. Targets without introspectable signatures (some C callables)
fall back to signature-based forwarding alone.

Fixes #261

subject: Fix off-by-one in Bits length check
problem_statement:
Fix off-by-one in Bits length check

The largest value representable in len_ bits is 2 ** len_ - 1, but the
guard used 'val > 2 ** len_', so Bits(4, 2) was accepted and produced a
3-bit value ('100') with a declared len of 2, silently breaking the
len/__getitem__ invariant and failing to round-trip. Use '>=' so a value
needing more than len_ bits raises, matching the guard's error message.
The auto-computed len_ branch never trips the stricter check.

subject: funcutils: forward defaulted and kw-only args as keywords in wraps invocations (#343)
problem_statement:
funcutils: forward defaulted and kw-only args as keywords in wraps invocations (#343)

Behavior change: wrappers built by funcutils.wraps now receive defaulted
(non-positional-only, non-pre-varargs) and keyword-only parameters in
**kwargs instead of *args. Wrappers that inspected *args positionally for
defaulted params must read **kwargs instead.

Two carve-outs keep existing calls working: positional-only params are
recovered from co_posonlyargcount and never keyword-forwarded (keywords
would be rejected outright), and every regular arg stays positional when
*varargs is present (keyword-forwarding an arg preceding *varargs
collides with non-empty varargs).

This also lifts the #261 limitation: wraps(g)(f) now works when f takes
keyword-only b and g takes defaulted positional b.

subject: fix(strutils): stop singularize() mangling words ending in 'ss'
problem_statement:
fix(strutils): stop singularize() mangling words ending in 'ss'

singularize() blindly stripped the trailing 's' from any word ending in
's' that did not match the earlier '-ies'/'-ses' branches, so words that
are already singular and end in a double 's' were corrupted:

    singularize('glass')  -> 'glas'
    singularize('boss')   -> 'bos'
    singularize('class')  -> 'clas'
    singularize('kiss')   -> 'kis'
    singularize('address')-> 'addres'

No English plural ends in 'ss' -- the plural of these words ends in
'sses' (glass -> glasses), which is already handled by the preceding
`word.endswith('es') and word[-3] == 's'` branch. This also broke the
idempotency implied by the function's own docstring, which states
singularize('Glasses') == 'Glass': feeding that canonical singular back
in produced 'Glas', and applying singularize() defensively to an
already-singular word degraded it further ('boss' -> 'bos' -> 'bo').

Fix: add an `elif word.endswith('ss')` guard before the final
`word[:-1]` fallback that returns the word unchanged. Real '-sses'
plurals are unaffected because that branch runs first, so
singularize('glasses') still returns 'glass'. The single-'s' ambiguous
cases (e.g. 'bus') are intentionally left alone; they are
indistinguishable from a regular plural without a dictionary.

Adds test_singularize_double_s covering the double-'s' singular words,
case preservation, the still-correct '-sses' plurals, and idempotency.

subject: Fix copy.copy/copy.deepcopy collapsing OrderedMultiDict values
problem_statement:
Fix copy.copy/copy.deepcopy collapsing OrderedMultiDict values

OrderedMultiDict subclasses dict, so the inherited __reduce_ex__ emits a
dictitems iterator over the underlying {key: [values]} dict. During
copy._reconstruct that iterator is replayed via __setitem__ after
__setstate__ has already rebuilt the multidict, overwriting each key's list
of values with a single value -- so copy.deepcopy(omd) != omd (and
copy.copy too).

__getstate__/__setstate__ already round-trip the full multi-value state
(pickle relied on them and was correct), so add __reduce__ returning a plain
(callable, args, state) tuple with no dictitems. copy, deepcopy and pickle
(protocols 0-5) now all preserve every value.

subject: Fix OrderedMultiDict equality to compare values against plain mappings
problem_statement:
Fix OrderedMultiDict equality to compare values against plain mappings

OrderedMultiDict.__eq__ has a branch for comparing against a non-OMD
mapping (anything with a keys() method, e.g. a dict). That branch
computes other[selfk] == self[selfk] but throws the result away, so it
only checks that every key of self exists in other and never compares
the values. As a result an OMD compares equal to any same-keyed mapping
regardless of the values:

    >>> omd = OMD([('a', 1), ('b', 2)])
    >>> omd == {'a': 999, 'b': 2}
    True   # should be False

The existing test_eq doesn't catch this because its dict case is written
as d == omd, which dispatches to dict.__eq__ rather than OMD.__eq__; the
buggy branch is only reached with the OMD on the left.

Compare the values and return False on mismatch. The same __eq__ is
duplicated in urlutils.OrderedMultiDict (used by QueryParamDict), so it's
fixed there too. Added regression tests for both.

subject: Adds cache option to remap and use in research
problem_statement:
Adds cache option to remap and use in research

There is a mismatch between the caching of transformed objects in the
`remap` function and the need for `research` to traverse all sub
trees. For most values this is inconsequential (like atomic ints,
etc.) but for small tuples (e.g. `("hello",)`) these get compiled as
the same value and return the same `id(...)`. In `remap` these get
cached and never get `enter` called on them and thus the hooks for
`research` to return the values never gets called.

In this fix an option to disable/enable the cache is introduced to the
`remap` function which simply disables using transformed values from
the cache. Then in the `research` function caching is turned off.

The existing `remap` behavior is maintained as caching by default is
turned on.

subject: Expose combined `__annotations__` on composed functions (#496) (#634)
problem_statement:
Expose combined `__annotations__` on composed functions (#496) (#634)

Expose combined annotations on composed functions (#634)

compose(g, f) now reports {'x': int, 'return': float} for
f: (x: int) -> str and g: (y: str) -> float, so typing.get_type_hints,
inspect.get_annotations, and functools.wraps see the view that
signature already gives: parameter annotations from the first function
applied, return annotation from the last.

The annotations are derived from inspect.signature, so partial, curry,
bound methods, classes, and nested compositions work, and callables
without a signature contribute nothing.  They are exposed through a
dict-subclass descriptor so Compose itself keeps an empty dict
annotations, which typing and inspect require before Python 3.14.

On Python 3.14+, Compose also has annotate, so functools.wraps copies
the annotations and the FORWARDREF and STRING formats work.

See #496.

returned the default instead of None, and it never got its LRU
position refreshed on read.

private sentinel default, so presence is checked directly rather than
inferred from the value.
